newsitem.title: USA: Victims' families celebrate verdict, pain lingers.
newsitem.headline: Victims' families celebrate verdict, pain lingers.

text.p: Cries of joy and relief broke an eerie silence in Oklahoma City's bomb-scarred downtown on Monday as Timothy McVeigh was declared guilty of planting the bomb that killed 168 people.

Bombing survivors and relatives of those killed joined about 300 city residents at the bombing site, celebrating McVeigh's conviction even though many said that justice would not take their pain away.
"I am sure there are 168 people who are smiling down on us from above," said Dan McKinney, whose wife, Linda, was killed in the bombing.

Donna McKinney, who was Linda's niece, said the verdict had taken a huge weight off her shoulders and that those hardest hit by the bombing had finally found justice after going through two years of hell. "We've lost so many people but at least he didn't get away with it."
Around her, scores of people hugged each other, wept and even knelt in prayer when the guilty verdict was relayed to Oklahoma City from the federal courtroom 600 miles (1,000 km) away in Denver.

Across town, bomb survivor Arlene Blanchard whooped with joy, jumped up and down and then sang "Amazing Grace" to her 5-month-old son with tears running down her face after hearing the verdict on her television set.

"Oh, thank you, Jesus," Blanchard cried as the first guilty verdict was read. She was in the Army recruiting office of the Alfred P. Murrah building when the bomb exploded, and suffered back and neck injuries.
But for many survivors, the joy of winning a conviction could not wipe out the pain of their loss.

Bud Welch, whose 23-year-old daughter Julie was killed in the bombing, went to the site of his daughter's death to hear the verdict but said he could not celebrate even though he was convinced McVeigh was guilty.
"I thought it would be all joy but it isn't," Welch said. "It's a very dull victory. The bottom line is that my little girl isn't coming back and I have the rest of my life to deal with that."
Ten yards (metres) behind him stood the grassy field where the building stood before McVeigh's truck bomb tore it to pieces on April 19, 1995.

While the Murrah building's battered remains were blown up in a controlled explosion months after the bombing, several surrounding buildings still stand across the street with huge holes blown out of them.

Most of the victims' relatives want McVeigh to be given the death penalty at the end of the trial's sentencing phase, which starts on Wednesday, but most concede that even that will not be enough to erase their loss.

"I supect that even if we get a death penalty, it is not going to make me feel any better. We'll have justice, but it is not going to change anything," said Sharon Medearis, whose husband Claude, a senior special agent of the U.S. Customs Service, was killed in the blast.
Nevertheless, survivors and relatives agreed that they were at least saved the misery of a mistrial or an acquittal, and all had words of praise for the jury and U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch.

"I am very proud of our Constitution, which has shown it can provide a trial that is appropriate even for McVeigh. We don't live in a vigilante society and this trial certainly represents a civilised nation seeking justice," bombing survivor Paul Heath said.
Dozens more family members gathered on Monday at an auditorium on the outskirts of Oklahoma City to watch the verdict on a two-way, closed-circuit feed direct from the Denver courthouse.
They said afterward that all those inside the auditorium stood up and began embracing each other as soon as the first verdicts came in.

"It felt really good. There was lots of crying and we started to cheer before the judge had adjourned so we had to sit down and be quiet again. But it was an incredible feeling," said Stephanie Titcomb, whose cousin Susan Ferrell was killed by the bomb.

After the verdict came in, several of those who were in the auditorium went down to the bombing site to say prayers around the "Survivor Tree," an elm which was badly charred by the bomb but survived and has become a symbol of the city's recovery.
"It is a symbol of life and we just wanted to come down here and give thanks to God," said John Taylor, who lost his 41-year-old daughter, Teresa Lauderdale, in the bombing.
